entities.name: Amasa Dana
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Amasa Dana (1792–1867) was an American Democratic politician from New York who served in the U.S. House (1845–1847 and 1847–1849) during the Polk administration — the era of the Mexican-American War, the Oregon boundary settlement with Britain, and the Walker Tariff. A New York Democrat, Dana served during the Wilmot Proviso controversy — the proposal to ban slavery from all territories acquired from Mexico that became the most divisive issue of the Polk years and a precursor to the Civil War sectional conflict.

New York's Democratic Party in this era was divided between the Hunker and Barnburner factions — conservative Democrats who accommodated the South versus antislavery Democrats who opposed slavery extension.

Dana's four-year House service contributed New York's Democratic voice to the Polk era's defining debates.

He was an Owego, New York lawyer and judge.
